explanations.explanation: That's the ask, baker. David prays, "Hide me from the scheming of the wicked, from the mob of workers of iniquity…" (Psalm 64:2). He doesn't open with a battle plan. He runs to God first. I think that's a pretty good place to start on a rough day.

explanations.answer: Give him an army to fight them
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, friend. A mob that big, you'd want some backup. But David never asks for soldiers in this psalm. He says, "Hide me from the scheming of the wicked…" (Psalm 64:2). He's asking God to cover him.

explanations.answer: Make them forget all about him
explanations.explanation: Ooh, that's a sneaky one, baker. Just slip out the back and hope nobody remembers you. David doesn't ask for that. He prays, "Hide me from the scheming of the wicked…" (Psalm 64:2). He wants to be hidden from their scheming, not wiped from their memory.
Tongues, baker! David says they "…sharpen their tongues like swords…" (Psalm 64:3). The sword is the comparison, and the tongue is what's being sharpened. Words can cut deep, and David knows it.

Spears sound right, don't they? Very battle-ready. But David says they "…sharpen their tongues like swords and aim their bitter words like arrows…" (Psalm 64:3). The swords and arrows are comparisons. The real weapon is their talk.
Whoa, friend, an axe? That's a lot of chopping. David never mentions one. He says they "…sharpen their tongues like swords…" (Psalm 64:3). The only thing being sharpened is their tongues.

That's it, baker. David says they are "…ambushing the innocent in seclusion, shooting suddenly, without fear." (Psalm 64:4). No warning and no worry on their side. That's what makes the ambush so sneaky.
If only, friend! A mob full of doubt would be a gentler mob. But David says they are "…shooting suddenly, without fear." (Psalm 64:4). They shoot suddenly, and fear isn't holding them back.

Not quite, friend. David says they are "…shooting suddenly, without fear." (Psalm 64:4). The verse says suddenly, not rarely, and it shows no regret at all. I think this one hurts, since it's the innocent who are ambushed.

Yes, baker. The verse says they speak of hiding their snares. Then the wicked say, "Who will see them?" (Psalm 64:5). That's the question they ask about their snares. I think they're hoping nobody does.
Not quite, friend. That sounds like people deciding who goes through a door first. The wicked ask, "Who will see them?" (Psalm 64:5). That question is about seeing, not about who steps in.

explanations.answer: Who will help us hide them
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, since they do speak of hiding their snares. But they don't ask for helpers. They say, "Who will see them?" (Psalm 64:5). I think they're hoping nobody will.
True, baker. The wicked say, "We have perfected a secret plan." (Psalm 64:6). Perfected! They think there are no loose ends. I've said that about a batch before it hit the floor.

Actually it's true, friend. The wicked say, "We have perfected a secret plan." (Psalm 64:6). That's their own claim about their plan. Then the psalm turns with, "But God will shoot them with arrows…" (Psalm 64:7).
I see why you'd think so, baker, but it's false. David never says he'll fight back himself. The psalm turns with "But God will shoot them with arrows…" (Psalm 64:7). God is the one who acts.

False is right, baker. Look at how the turn goes: "But God will shoot them with arrows; suddenly they will be wounded." (Psalm 64:7). David isn't grabbing a weapon. He hands the whole thing to God, and I think that's a relief.

Arrows, baker! David says, "But God will shoot them with arrows…" (Psalm 64:7). Remember how David said the mob aims their bitter words like arrows? Now God is the one who shoots. The verse goes on, "suddenly they will be wounded." (Psalm 64:7).

Stones are a fair guess, friend. But David doesn't say that. The verse reads, "But God will shoot them with arrows…" (Psalm 64:7). It's arrows, and David also uses arrows as a picture for the mob's bitter words (Psalm 64:3).
Fire! I'd know a thing or two about that, friend, with all my ovens. But this verse isn't about fire. It says, "But God will shoot them with arrows…" (Psalm 64:7). Arrows are the answer.

That's right, baker. David says, "They will be made to stumble, their own tongues turned against them." (Psalm 64:8). Remember the tongues sharpened like swords back in verse 3? Those same tongues are turned against them.

explanations.answer: They'll be taught to praise God
explanations.explanation: That's a kind thought, friend. But it isn't what David says. The verse reads, "…their own tongues turned against them." (Psalm 64:8). Their tongues end up working against them.

explanations.answer: They'll be kept quiet for good
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, friend, but the verse doesn't say they're silenced. David says, "They will be made to stumble, their own tongues turned against them." (Psalm 64:8). Their own tongues are turned against them, and that's what the verse tells us.
You got it, baker. "Then all mankind will fear and proclaim the work of God…" (Psalm 64:9). People see what God has done, and they can't keep quiet about it. They're talking about Him.

Not this crowd, friend. David says, "Then all mankind will fear and proclaim the work of God; so they will ponder what He has done." (Psalm 64:9). Pondering means they're thinking over what God has done. That's fearing and proclaiming, not laughing.

explanations.answer: Run and hide from the wicked
explanations.explanation: Good thought, baker, but David says the wicked are the ones who will be wounded and made to stumble. He says all mankind will "…fear and proclaim the work of God…" (Psalm 64:9). They're looking at what God did, not running from the mob.

explanations.answer: Rejoice and take refuge in the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the ending, baker. "Let the righteous rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in Him…" (Psalm 64:10). David began by asking God to hide him, and he finishes by saying the righteous can run to God and be glad. It's a full circle.

explanations.answer: Keep quiet and wait for the LORD to act
explanations.explanation: I see where that comes from, friend, because David does leave the action to God. But the last verse says, "Let the righteous rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in Him…" (Psalm 64:10). It ends with rejoicing, not hushed waiting.

explanations.answer: Fight back in the name of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's a tough-sounding ending, baker, but it isn't this one. David closes with, "Let the righteous rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in Him…" (Psalm 64:10). No swords come out. The righteous rejoice and run to Him.
